title: Bhūr annam: the vyāhṛti offerings with food
theme: The three great utterances, each joined to the deity of its world, used in offerings for food; closed with homage to the gods and the fathers.

words.role: the deity of the earth, as the commentator explains
words.context: Anonymous: «भूः पृथिव्यधिष्ठानदेवता» — the deity presiding over the earth
Anonymous: «चरुरूपमन्नं» — food in the form of the boiled offering

words.meaning: svāhā — the call that ends an offering
svadhā — the call used for the ancestors

words.role: with bhuvaḥ and suvaḥ, the subject of the closing formula

sandhi.type: visarga after ū before a vowel; final m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: A visarga after a vowel other than a/ā becomes r before a vowel (bhūr annam); a final m joins a following vowel (annam agnaye).
-aḥ before a becomes -o and the a is elided, marked by avagraha: bhuvaḥ + annam → bhuvo ’nnam (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)).
After -e an initial a is elided (avagraha): vāyave ’ntarikṣāya (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)).
suvaḥ (svar) keeps its r before a vowel: suvar annam; then annam ādityāya.
The visarga before s is written as a doubled s in the Taittirīya recitation: digbhyas svāhā.

sandhi.type: aḥ before a voiced consonant; ūḥ before a voiced consonant; visarga before s
sandhi.rule: -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant (pitṛbhyo bhūḥ); bhūḥ becomes bhūr before b; bhuvaḥ before s is written bhuvas s (Taittirīya doubling); suvaḥ keeps its r before a vowel (suvar annam), and annam joins om (annam om).

morphology.note: The three vyāhṛtis bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ are indeclinable words naming earth, mid-air and heaven. Bhāskara recalls that Prajāpati uttered them to make those worlds: «स भूरिति व्याहरत् । स भूमिमसृजत».
An indeclinable; it does not take the dative constructions around it as its object, which is why Bhāskara notes that the dative is not governed by it: «स्वाहाकारसम्बन्धेऽपि निपातत्वाच् चतुर्थ्यभावः».
The exclamation used in offerings to the ancestors, as svāhā is used for the gods.

translation.literal: Earth: food to Agni, to the earth, svāhā. Mid-air: food to Vāyu, to the mid-air, svāhā. Heaven: food to Āditya, to the sky, svāhā. Earth, mid-air, heaven: food to the moon, to the quarters, svāhā. Homage to the gods; svadhā to the fathers. Earth, mid-air, heaven: food — om.
translation.readable: With the words for earth, mid-air and heaven, food is offered to Agni and the earth, to the wind and the mid-air, to the sun and the sky, and with all three together to the moon and the quarters. Homage to the gods, svadhā to the ancestors. Earth, mid-air, heaven: may there be food — so be it.

syntax: A string of verbless offering formulas. Each has the same frame: a vyāhṛti, the word annam, two datives (a deity and its region) and svāhā. The fourth joins all three vyāhṛtis to the moon and the quarters. Two salutations follow (namo devebhyaḥ, svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ), and the three vyāhṛtis return with annam and om.

ambiguities.note: Annam may be the thing offered or the thing prayed for. The anonymous commentator reads both: the deity of the world should give food, and food in the form of the boiled offering is offered to it («मह्यमन्नं दद्यादिति शेषः । तदर्थं च चरुरूपमन्नं मयाऽस्मिन्स्मार्ताग्नौ स्वाहा सुहुतमस्तु»).

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose offering formulas (yajus), one printed line of 68 syllables; no metre is claimed.

beginner: This anuvāka is a set of short offering formulas built on the three “great utterances”, bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ and suvaḥ, the old names for earth, the space between, and heaven. Each formula pairs one of these with the god of that world (fire for earth, wind for the space between, the sun for heaven) and adds the word for food and the call svāhā, said when something is placed into a sacred fire. A fourth formula uses all three together for the moon and the quarters. Then come a greeting to the gods and the word svadhā for the ancestors, and the three utterances once more with food and om, “so be it”. The commentators explain it as a fire-offering made by someone who wishes for food; this record reports that explanation and claims no result for it.
analogy: Like a letter addressed in turn to three households and then to all of them together, each line names the place, the one who lives there, and the gift.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It offers food, with svāhā, to Agni and the earth under bhūḥ, to Vāyu and the mid-air under bhuvaḥ, to Āditya and the sky under suvaḥ, and to the moon and the quarters under all three; it greets the gods and the fathers, and closes with the three vyāhṛtis, food and om.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator calls these homa mantras for one who wishes for food, offered as part of removing sin: «अतः परं पापक्षयार्थद्वाराऽन्नकामस्य होममन्त्रानाह». He describes the procedure in the domestic fire according to one’s own gṛhya rules, and has the worshipper face east for namo devebhyaḥ and south for svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ. Sāyaṇa, whose order differs, treats the passage as a variant of the plain vyāhṛti offerings for one who wants plentiful food: «अन्नसमृद्धिकामस्य तेष्वेव मन्त्रेषु पाठान्तरमाह».

commentary.q: What does the closing om mean here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator takes om as assent: the three deities agree to give the food prayed for — «ओंकारोऽभ्यनुज्ञां कथयति» and «अस्मत्प्रार्थितमन्नं दातुं भूर्भुवः सुवस्तिस्रो देवता ओम्».

commentary.q: How does Bhāskara read the same words?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara reads these anuvākas not as homa mantras for food but as meditation on the vyāhṛtis as Brahman. Here food is meditated on as Brahman in the form of bliss: «आनन्दब्रह्मणा ताद्रूप्येण व्याहृत्यादीनामुपासनामात्रम् अत्रानुवाके विशेषः». He introduces this anuvāka and the two around it together as the great vyāhṛtis that set out Brahman: «भूरग्नय इत्याद्यास्त्रयोऽनुवाका व्यष्टिसमष्टिरूपेण ब्रह्मण एव प्रतिपादका महाव्याहृतिनामानः». The two readings are reported side by side; the text itself only states the formulas.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The three witnesses agree on the words; the differences listed on the sources page for this anuvāka are spelling only (the doubled sibilant after a visarga against ः, and the like).

schools.disagreement: The commentaries on this text are ritual and Vedic, not Vedānta-school commentaries, and none of them takes a position here on which the Vedānta schools divide. No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available here). The difference that matters is between the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa, who read a homa for food, and Bhāskara, who reads a meditation on Brahman.

contemporary.text: The formulas name, in order, the ground, the air and the sky before naming food: what nourishes is traced back to the whole world that produces it. Pausing before a meal to name where it came from is a habit that needs no rite. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might each line name both a god and a region of the world, rather than only one?
reflect.deeper: The anonymous commentator reads a homa for food; Bhāskara reads a meditation on Brahman as bliss. What in the wording supports each?
reflect.practice: Before a meal, name three things that had to happen for it to reach you.

references.text: Sāyaṇa’s order differs from this text: his anuvāka 3 gives this passage as a variant reading of the plain vyāhṛti offerings (this edition’s 10.4), whose own comment, his anuvāka 2, is not in the copy used.

flags.note: Whether the formulas are offerings for food (the anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa) or a meditation on the vyāhṛtis as Brahman (Bhāskara) is a matter of commentary, not settled by the words.
